---
title: "Recovering the EZ diffusion model on the standard grid"
---

```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  fig.width = 7,
  fig.height = 4,
  out.width = "100%"
)
options(width = 90)
# paths relative to the package root, whether this renders from the
# package root (pkgdown) or from vignettes/articles
from_root <- function(path) {
  if (dir.exists("vignettes")) path else file.path("..", "..", path)
}
# the code shown is read from the script that produced the results
shown <- function(label, file) {
  lines <- readLines(from_root(file))
  markers <- grep("^## ---- ", lines)
  start <- markers[lines[markers] == paste("## ----", label)]
  end <- c(markers[markers > start], length(lines) + 1L)[[1L]] - 1L
  code <- lines[(start + 1L):end]
  while (length(code) > 0L && !nzchar(trimws(code[[length(code)]]))) {
    code <- code[-length(code)]
  }
  code
}
script <- "vignettes/articles/precompute/recovery-ezdm.R"
script_url <- paste0(
  "https://github.com/GidonFrischkorn/bmmtools/blob/main/", script
)
fmt <- function(x, digits = 2) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = digits)
library(bmmtools)
```

```{r data, include = FALSE}
res <- readRDS(from_root("vignettes/articles/assets/recovery-ezdm.rds"))
bmm_version <- res$toolchain[["bmm"]]
reps <- length(unique(res$cells$replication))
cells <- res$cells
pop <- res$population
sds <- res$families$sd
subj <- res$families$subject
rel <- res$reliability
rel <- rel[match(
  paste(subj$condition, subj$term), paste(rel$condition, rel$term)
), ]
cors <- res$correlations
readoff <- res$readoff
rows <- as.data.frame(res$out)
# one row of a table, by design and term; anything but exactly one row is
# an error, so a regenerated asset cannot silently shift the prose
pick <- function(x, n, t, term = NULL) {
  keep <- x$n_subjects == n & x$n_trials == t
  if (!is.null(term)) keep <- keep & x$term == term
  out <- x[keep, ]
  stopifnot(nrow(out) == 1L)
  out
}
smallest <- function(n, threshold, column = "smallest_with_coverage") {
  out <- readoff[readoff$n_subjects == n & readoff$threshold == threshold, ]
  stopifnot(nrow(out) == 1L)
  out[[column]]
}
# Monte Carlo standard error of a rate from `reps` replications
mcse <- function(p, n = reps) sqrt(p * (1 - p) / n)
pm <- function(p) paste0(fmt(p), " ± ", fmt(mcse(p)))
with_mcse <- function(x, se) paste0(fmt(x), " ± ", fmt(se, 3))
pars <- res$pars
accuracy <- stats::plogis(pars[["drift"]] * exp(pars[["bound"]]))
mean_rt <- exp(pars[["ndt"]]) + exp(pars[["bound"]]) /
  (2 * pars[["drift"]]) * tanh(pars[["drift"]] * exp(pars[["bound"]]) / 2)
n_pass <- sum(cells$converged)
n_pass_101 <- sum(cells$converged_101)
# population coverage pooled over every design
pop_rows <- rows[rows$level == "population", ]
pooled_coverage <- mean(pop_rows$covered)
# how far the converged-only summary moves r_low
conv_subj <- res$families_converged$subject
r_low_shift <- max(abs(
  conv_subj$r_low[match(
    paste(subj$condition, subj$term),
    paste(conv_subj$condition, conv_subj$term)
  )] - subj$r_low
))
# the generating correlation of 0.4, and the in-sample correlations
cor_rows <- as.data.frame(attr(res$out, "correlations"))
in_sample <- tapply(
  cor_rows$sample_value, paste(cor_rows$condition, cor_rows$term), mean
)
cors$in_sample <- in_sample[paste(cors$condition, cors$term)]
target <- cors[cors$true_value == 0.4, ]
# the lower end of a 95 % Wilson interval at 10 of 10
wilson_all <- unique(pop$coverage_wilson_low[pop$coverage == 1])
# posterior SD over prior SD at the smallest contraction
sd_ratio <- sqrt(1 - min(pop$contraction, na.rm = TRUE))
readoff <- readoff[order(readoff$n_subjects, readoff$threshold), ]
pair_label <- c(
  bound__drift = "drift – bound", bound__ndt = "bound – ndt",
  drift__ndt = "drift – ndt"
)
# the prose below states these; a regenerated asset must still satisfy them
stopifnot(
  reps == 10,
  smallest(50, 0.8) == 300, smallest(50, 0.7) == 300,
  smallest(50, 0.7, "smallest") == 100, smallest(20, 0.7) == 100,
  is.na(smallest(50, 0.9)), smallest(20, 0.8) == 300,
  smallest(20, 0.8, "smallest_point") == 100,
  pick(pop, 50, 100, "bound")$coverage == 0.8,
  pick(pop, 50, 300, "bound")$coverage == 0.9,
  length(wilson_all) == 1L,
  !pick(pop, 50, 100, "bound")$coverage_ok,
  all(pop$coverage_ok[pop$n_trials == 300]),
  all(abs(pop$bias) < 0.05),
  all(subj$r[subj$term == "drift"] < subj$r[subj$term == "bound"]),
  pick(subj, 50, 100, "drift")$r_low < 0.8,
  pick(subj, 50, 300, "drift")$r_low >= 0.8,
  all(cells$status == "ok"),
  all(target$coverage >= 0.9)
)
```

This page reports one parameter recovery study: the three-parameter EZ
diffusion model, `bmm::ezdm()`, fitted with bmm `r bmm_version`. Data
were simulated from known parameter values, the model was fitted to
them, and the estimates were compared with the values that generated
the data. A researcher planning an EZ diffusion study can read from it
how well each parameter is recovered with 20 or 50 subjects and 30, 100
or 300 trials per subject, and how many trials per person an analysis of
individual differences needs. The page does not say how many subjects a
study of group means or of correlations between parameters needs; it
shows only what 20 and 50 subjects give.

The page is provisional. bmmtools plans a *validation card* for each
model it supports: a standard report, rerun for every bmm release, that
applies the same checks to the same set of designs, the *standard grid*
used here
([issue #21](https://github.com/GidonFrischkorn/bmmtools/issues/21)).
The card for `ezdm` will replace this page. Some numbers below,
uncertainties of rates, the reliability of the subject estimates and the
smallest design that meets a target, are computed by hand with the
formula stated each time, because the page was written before
`summary()` of a recovery result and `smallest_design()` reported them
([issue #17](https://github.com/GidonFrischkorn/bmmtools/issues/17)).

Two words recur. A *design* is one combination of subjects and trials;
the grid has six. Each design was simulated and fitted
`r reps` times, the *replications*, so the study has
`r nrow(cells)` fits. The page reads every number from the stored
results of those fits, so it needs no Stan to build.

## The model and the generating values

```{r model, eval = FALSE, code = shown("model", script)}
```

Each parameter is estimated on its *link scale*, the unbounded scale
the model works on: `drift` as it is, `bound` and `ndt` as logarithms,
so a between-subject SD of 0.2 on `ndt` means people differ by about
20 % in non-decision time. The three-parameter EZ model fixes `s`, the
within-trial noise of the diffusion process, to 1. At these population
values a person answers correctly on `r fmt(100 * accuracy, 1)` % of
trials, with a mean response time of `r fmt(mean_rt, 2)` s (the
EZ expressions for accuracy and mean response time with `s = 1`).

*Contraction* says how much the data narrowed a posterior relative to
its prior: 1 − (posterior SD / prior SD)². It is near 1 when the data
determine the estimate and near 0 when the posterior is still the prior.
`prior_sd` gives the prior SD of each parameter under bmm's default
priors: a normal prior's SD is its second argument, and an exponential
prior with rate λ has SD 1/λ. `drift` has no row, because its default
prior on the population value is a Cauchy distribution, which has no
SD; its contraction stays empty.

## The run

```{r run, eval = FALSE, code = shown("run", script)}
```

`reps = 10` is the number of replications per design. `re_cor = "all"`
lets the model estimate all three between-subject correlations.
`levels` and `correlations = "model"` choose what is compared with the
truth: the population means, the between-subject SDs, every subject's
parameters, and the model's correlation estimates. `seed` fixes the
simulated data and the sampler's seed, and the arguments after it go to
`bmm::bmm()`. It does not make the fits identical: a second run of this
script gave estimates that differ in the third decimal, most likely
because bmm draws the chains' starting values from R's random number
generator, which `seed` does not set.
`fits_dir` is a folder for the fitted models, set at the top of the
script; `?recovery_grid` explains the rest.

Fitting took `r fmt(res$minutes_fitting, 1)` minutes in all (bmm
`r bmm_version`, CmdStan `r res$toolchain[["cmdstan"]]`), between
`r fmt(min(cells$fit_seconds), 1)` and
`r fmt(max(cells$fit_seconds), 1)` seconds per fit.

Every fit goes through bmmtools' convergence gate. It checks every
parameter of the fit, the between-subject correlations and each
person's values included. R-hat compares the chains and should be close
to 1. The effective sample size (ESS) counts how many independent draws
the chains are worth. Divergent transitions are steps where the sampler
failed. The gate's defaults are R-hat at most 1.05, bulk and tail ESS at
least 400, and at most 10 divergent transitions, so a fit with a few
divergences can still pass. `r n_pass` of the
`r nrow(cells)` fits pass; `r n_pass_101` pass if R-hat must also be at
most 1.01.

```{r convergence, echo = FALSE}
by_design <- split(cells, ~ n_subjects + n_trials)
tab <- do.call(rbind, lapply(by_design, function(d) {
  data.frame(
    subjects = d$n_subjects[[1]], trials = d$n_trials[[1]],
    `fits passing the gate` = sum(d$converged),
    `passing with R-hat ≤ 1.01` = sum(d$converged_101),
    `fits with any divergence` = sum(d$n_divergent > 0),
    `median seconds per fit` = fmt(stats::median(d$fit_seconds), 1),
    check.names = FALSE
  )
}))
knitr::kable(
  tab[order(tab$subjects, tab$trials), ],
  row.names = FALSE, align = "r"
)
```

Most fits that fail are at 30 trials. In the fits that failed, the
parameter with the lowest ESS was usually a between-subject correlation,
not a population mean. The tables below use every fit. Using only the
fits that pass the gate moves no `r_low` value (defined below) by more
than `r fmt(r_low_shift, 3)` and changes none of the conclusions.

## Population means and between-subject SDs

For each fit the estimate is the posterior median. *Bias* is the mean,
over the ten replications, of estimate minus generating value; *RMSE* is
the root of the mean squared difference; *CrI width* is the mean width
of the 95 % credible interval (CrI). All three are on the link scale.
*Coverage* is the share of the ten replications whose 95 % CrI contains
the generating value. Its Monte Carlo standard error (MCSE) is
`sqrt(p (1 - p) / 10)` at the observed rate `p`, so a coverage of 0.90
has an MCSE of `r fmt(mcse(0.9), 3)`. At a coverage of 1.00 that
formula gives 0, which does not mean the coverage is known exactly: ten
covered intervals out of ten are still consistent with a true coverage
as low as `r fmt(wilson_all, 2)` (the lower end of a 95 % Wilson
interval for a rate). Read every "1.00 ± 0.00" below that way.

```{r population, echo = FALSE}
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  subjects = pop$n_subjects, trials = pop$n_trials, parameter = pop$term,
  bias = fmt(pop$bias, 3), RMSE = fmt(pop$rmse, 3),
  `coverage ± MCSE` = pm(pop$coverage),
  `CrI width` = fmt(pop$ci_width, 3),
  contraction = ifelse(
    is.na(pop$contraction), "–", fmt(pop$contraction, 3)
  ),
  check.names = FALSE
), row.names = FALSE, align = "r")
```

The population means are recovered without visible bias: at most
`r fmt(max(abs(pop$bias)), 3)` in absolute value, about a tenth of
drift's between-subject SD of 0.3; for `bound` and `ndt`, on the log
scale, a bias of 0.01 is an error of about 1 %. The contraction of
`bound` and `ndt` is at least
`r fmt(min(pop$contraction, na.rm = TRUE), 3)`, which means a posterior
SD at most `r fmt(sd_ratio, 2)` times the prior SD: the data, not the
prior, locate them even with 20 subjects and 30 trials. Coverage of a
single design ranges from `r fmt(min(pop$coverage), 1)` to
`r fmt(max(pop$coverage), 1)`, and ten replications cannot tell 0.90
from the nominal 0.95. Pooled over the 3 parameters, 6 designs and 10
replications, `r sum(pop_rows$covered)` of `r nrow(pop_rows)` intervals
cover, a coverage of
`r fmt(pooled_coverage, 3)` ± `r fmt(mcse(0.95, nrow(pop_rows)), 3)`
(the MCSE that this many intervals of the right width would have),
which is consistent with intervals of the right width.

The between-subject SDs are read the same way, on the link scale:

```{r sd, echo = FALSE}
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  subjects = sds$n_subjects, trials = sds$n_trials, parameter = sds$term,
  bias = fmt(sds$bias, 3), RMSE = fmt(sds$rmse, 3),
  `coverage ± MCSE` = pm(sds$coverage), `CrI width` = fmt(sds$ci_width, 3),
  contraction = fmt(sds$contraction, 3),
  check.names = FALSE
), row.names = FALSE, align = "r")
```

Their bias is at most `r fmt(max(abs(sds$bias)), 3)` and their
contraction at least `r fmt(min(sds$contraction), 3)`.

## Subject parameters

Here each person's estimate is compared with that person's generating
value. Within one replication, *r* is the correlation between estimated
and generating values across the people. The ten values of r are
averaged after Fisher's z transformation, which makes correlations
safe to average, and *r_low* is the lower end of the usual 95 %
interval of that average, `tanh(z ± 1.96 / sqrt(N))` with `N` the sum of
(people − 3) over the replications. The two reliability columns are
computed by hand on the link scale, per replication, then averaged, with
their MCSE (the SD over replications divided by √10). With `m` the
posterior means of the people and `v` their posterior variances:

- *reliability from the truth* is the squared correlation of `m` with
  the generating values;
- *reliability from the model* is `var(m) / (var(m) + mean(v))`, which
  needs no generating values and so can be computed on real data;
- *gap* is the second minus the first, per replication, then averaged.

```{r subject, echo = FALSE}
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  subjects = subj$n_subjects, trials = subj$n_trials, parameter = subj$term,
  r = fmt(subj$r), r_low = fmt(subj$r_low),
  `reliability from the truth` =
    with_mcse(rel$reliability_true, rel$reliability_true_mcse),
  `reliability from the model` =
    with_mcse(rel$reliability_model, rel$reliability_model_mcse),
  gap = with_mcse(rel$reliability_gap, rel$reliability_gap_mcse),
  check.names = FALSE
), row.names = FALSE, align = "r")
```

`bound` and `ndt` are recovered well from 30 trials on
(r ≥ `r fmt(min(subj$r[subj$term != "drift"]))`). `drift` is the hard
parameter: with 50 subjects its r is
`r fmt(pick(subj, 50, 30, "drift")$r)` at 30 trials,
`r fmt(pick(subj, 50, 100, "drift")$r)` at 100 and
`r fmt(pick(subj, 50, 300, "drift")$r)` at 300. More people do not make
each person's estimate better: at 30 trials drift's r is
`r fmt(pick(subj, 20, 30, "drift")$r)` with 20 subjects and
`r fmt(pick(subj, 50, 30, "drift")$r)` with 50. From 100 trials on, the
reliability from the model differs from the reliability from the truth
by at most `r fmt(max(abs(rel$reliability_gap[rel$n_trials >= 100])), 3)`;
at 30 trials it is lower in
`r sum(rel$reliability_gap[rel$n_trials == 30] < 0)` of the 6 rows.

## The correlation between drift and boundary

The simulation drew each person's drift rate and boundary separation
from a population in which they correlate 0.4, and left the other two
pairs uncorrelated. In a sample of 20 or 50 people the correlation of
the drawn values differs from 0.4 by chance; the column *in sample*
gives its mean over the ten replications. *Mean estimate* is the mean of
the posterior medians. *Coverage* is of the generating value, 0.4 or
0. *CrI excludes 0* is the share of replications whose 95 % CrI does not
contain zero: for the 0.4 pair, the chance that a study of this size
shows the correlation to differ from zero (its power).

```{r correlations, echo = FALSE}
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  subjects = cors$n_subjects, trials = cors$n_trials,
  pair = pair_label[cors$term], generating = fmt(cors$true_value, 1),
  `in sample` = fmt(cors$in_sample),
  `mean estimate` = fmt(cors$mean_estimate),
  `coverage ± MCSE` = pm(cors$coverage),
  `CrI width` = fmt(cors$ci_width),
  `CrI excludes 0` = fmt(cors$rejection_rate, 1),
  check.names = FALSE
), row.names = FALSE, align = "r")
```

The CrIs of the 0.4 correlation contain it in nine or ten of the ten
replications at every design, but they are
`r fmt(min(target$ci_width))` to `r fmt(max(target$ci_width))` wide, so
they say little about its size. They exclude zero in at most
`r fmt(max(target$rejection_rate[target$n_subjects == 50]), 1)` of the
replications with 50 subjects and
`r fmt(max(target$rejection_rate[target$n_subjects == 20]), 1)` with 20.
With 20 subjects and 30 trials the estimate is pulled towards zero
(`r fmt(pick(target, 20, 30)$mean_estimate)` against an in-sample
`r fmt(pick(target, 20, 30)$in_sample)`). With 20 subjects and 100
trials the estimate is low as well, but so were the correlations drawn
in those ten samples. A power of 0.7 at best means that a study with 50
people misses a correlation of 0.4 between drift and boundary about one
time in three.

## How many trials?

The validation cards will answer this question with one rule. Take a
bar for r_low, 0.80 by default, a common convention for measures used
to rank individuals; the cards also report 0.70 and 0.90 for readers
with another bar. The answer is the smallest number of trials at which
r_low reaches the bar for every parameter, and stays there at every
larger number of trials in the grid. There is one more condition: at
that design, the coverage of every population mean must lie within one
MCSE of 0.95, with the MCSE taken at 0.95,
`sqrt(0.95 × 0.05 / 10)` = `r fmt(res$coverage_mcse, 3)`; with ten
replications, 9 or 10 covered intervals out of 10 pass. The condition
is there because a design at which the population intervals are too
narrow would be a poor recommendation, however well it ranks people.

A worked example with 50 subjects and the bar at 0.80: at 100 trials
drift's r_low is `r fmt(pick(subj, 50, 100, "drift")$r_low)`, below the
bar; at 300 it is `r fmt(pick(subj, 50, 300, "drift")$r_low)`, and
`bound` and `ndt` are above 0.80 already at fewer trials. The coverage
condition holds at 300 trials, so the answer is 300.

The column *using r* applies the same rule to r instead of r_low. Where
the two differ, the point estimate meets the bar but ten replications
are too few to be sure that it does. This page applies the rule by hand
([the code](`r script_url`), section `read-off`); in the package,
`smallest_design()` reads a target off a grid summary
([issue #17](https://github.com/GidonFrischkorn/bmmtools/issues/17)).

```{r readoff, echo = FALSE}
in_grid <- function(x) ifelse(is.na(x), "not reached in this grid", x)
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  subjects = readoff$n_subjects, bar = fmt(readoff$threshold, 2),
  `smallest number of trials` = in_grid(readoff$smallest_with_coverage),
  `using r` = in_grid(readoff$smallest_point),
  check.names = FALSE
), row.names = FALSE, align = "r")
```

With 50 subjects and bmm `r bmm_version`, a study needs
**`r smallest(50, 0.8)` trials** per person for an r_low of at least
0.80 on every parameter; 0.90 is not reached with 300 trials. The grid
has nothing between its trial counts, so "300" means more than 100 and
at most 300. `drift` decides the r_low part of each answer: `bound` and
`ndt` reach 0.80 at 100 and 30 trials (see the subject parameters).
The 0.80 answer is safe on r_low (drift's
`r fmt(pick(subj, 50, 300, "drift")$r_low)` at 300 trials is well above
the bar), but not on coverage: `bound` covered in
`r 10 * pick(pop, 50, 300, "bound")$coverage` of 10 replications at that
design, and one more miss would turn the answer into "not reached in
this grid".

The answer at 0.70 shows how much ten replications can decide. By r_low
alone it is `r smallest(50, 0.7, "smallest")` trials (drift's r_low is
`r fmt(pick(subj, 50, 100, "drift")$r_low)` at 100 trials). But at that
design the CrI of `bound`'s population mean covered in
`r 10 * pick(pop, 50, 100, "bound")$coverage` of 10 replications, outside
the one-MCSE band, so the rule moves on to `r smallest(50, 0.7)` trials.
With one more covered interval the answer would have been 100, and a
second run of this script, with different starting values, gave exactly
that. Read the 0.70 answer as "100 or 300", and the coverage at 50
subjects and 100 trials as a reason to look closer, not as a failure:
pooled over all designs the intervals have the right width.

The number of subjects hardly matters for these answers: from 100
trials on, r is the same with 20 and with 50 people (see the subject
parameters). More people narrow the interval of r and of the population
estimates; they do not measure each person better. With 20 subjects the
answers are `r smallest(20, 0.7)` trials at 0.70
and `r smallest(20, 0.8)` at 0.80. At the 0.80 bar, r alone would say
100 trials: drift's r at 20 subjects and 100 trials is
`r fmt(pick(subj, 20, 100, "drift")$r)`, but its r_low is
`r fmt(pick(subj, 20, 100, "drift")$r_low)`.

## Reproducing the study

[`vignettes/articles/precompute/recovery-ezdm.R`](`r script_url`) runs
the grid and writes the results this page reads, to
`vignettes/articles/assets/recovery-ezdm.rds`. It needs bmm
`r bmm_version` or later, brms, cmdstanr and CmdStan.
